_comment: Reading-lens registry rendered by assets/lenses.js on read.html, dossier.html and replay.html. A reading lens is a PUBLISHED coherence method rendered as UI scaffolding: the site describes the method (site-authored prose, labeled ~ Nuanced with its sources) and gives the reader a place to apply it — it never asserts what a verse means and never fills in a reader's answer. kind=data-backed: transcribed source material exists (Khan outlines in data/exercises.json; coverage.surahs here MUST equal the set of transcribed outline surahs — scripts/check-lenses.mjs enforces it, and it grows only by transcribing an outline through the maintainer guide's Transcription Gate). kind=blank-worksheet: method questions only — site-authored prompts informed by the cited published descriptions of the method, never the scholars' own text; answers are the reader's own and never carry a verification badge. kind=empty-overlay: the reader marks their own candidate structure; the site asserts none. kind=context-panel: bundled reference data rendered read-only (conventional chronology, computed proper-noun counts) above the same kind of reader-answered questions — the data panels carry their own badges, and the questions follow the blank-worksheet rules. methodHtml and coverage.statementHtml are trusted site-authored HTML, never API or user text. Body rendering in assets/lenses.js dispatches by lens id, so a new entry needs a body function there. These reading lenses are distinct from index.html's daily-card 'lens', which is a rotating corpus statistic. Human TODO (not yet added, per the no-guessed-citations rule): bibliographic entries for Hashmi's Exordium and the English oaths study await confirmed publisher/year details before any lens may cite them; likewise no sirah or asbab al-nuzul source is registered yet, so the history lens's sirah section is a blank worksheet.

lenses.name: Sectional outline (Khan)
lenses.methodHtml: Irfan Ahmad Khan reads each surah as one continuous address and outlines it section by section, so the reader can follow the discourse as a whole rather than verse by verse in isolation. On this site his transcribed outlines are worked as exercises: propose your own structure first, then compare it against his published outline.

coverage.statementHtml: Six surahs have transcribed outlines so far — five from Khan's 2011 volume and one (al-'Asr) from his 2013 volume, whose thirty outlines cover surahs 85–114. The rest of that range is listed under wanted transcriptions; for surahs 1–84 no Khan outline exists at all, and the site asserts no structure it cannot cite.

lenses.name: ʿAmūd worksheet (Farahi–Islahi)
lenses.methodHtml: In the Farahi–Islahi school of nazm (coherence) reading, every surah has an ʿamūd — a central theme, literally a 'pillar', around which the whole surah turns — and each part of the surah is read in relation to it. The prompts below are site-authored study questions informed by that published method as described in Mustansir Mir's 1986 study; they are not Farahi's or Islahi's own text, and no ʿamūd statement is transcribed for any surah. The answers are yours.

questions.prompt: State, in one sentence, a candidate ʿamūd for this surah — what is the whole address about?
How does the opening introduce it? Which words, images, or oaths set the frame?
Walk the surah's sections: how does each relate to your candidate ʿamūd? Note any verse that resists it.
Does the closing return to, or resolve, the theme the opening raised?
Islahi reads most surahs as one of a pair. Does an adjacent surah treat the same theme from another side?
Restate your ʿamūd now. What changed since your first attempt, and which verses forced the change?

coverage.statementHtml: Blank worksheet only: the site transcribes no ʿamūd statement for any of the 114 surahs, and your answers are saved in this browser, never auto-filled, and never carry a verification badge.

lenses.name: Ring overlay (Cuypers / Farrin)
lenses.methodHtml: Michel Cuypers and Raymond Farrin document concentric composition in the Qur'an — members arranged A B C B′ A′ around a centre, following Semitic-rhetoric analysis. The overlay below is a blank frame for that method: pair up candidate members yourself and propose a centre.

coverage.statementHtml: Empty overlay only: no ring analysis exists anywhere on this site for any surah — adding one would mean transcribing a page-cited published analysis, not running a computation. The site's own mechanical symmetry proxies returned no surviving result in any surah; see the test on Patterns.

lenses.name: Historical context (when · who · sirah)
lenses.methodHtml: Reading a surah against where it sits in the revelation's unfolding — early or late, Meccan or Medinan — is a long-standing practice in Qur'anic study. This lens shows the conventional chronology the site already carries and the proper names the surah actually uses, then hands the sirah questions to you. The site registers no sirah or asbab al-nuzul (occasions of revelation) source, so it asserts nothing about the historical moment itself: that reading is yours to build from sources you consult yourself.

questions.prompt: From the sirah sources you consult (this site registers none), what was the community facing at the point where this surah is conventionally placed?
Who is being addressed — believers, opponents, the Prophet himself? What in the wording tells you?
Which earlier-prophet stories or events does the surah retell or allude to, and why might they land in this moment? The name list above only shows who is named — the reading is yours.
Does the conventional period label fit the surah's tone and themes as you read them? Note any verse that resists it.
Record which sirah or occasions-of-revelation source you used, with edition and page — the same citation discipline this site applies to itself.

coverage.statementHtml: Covers all 114 surahs for the conventional revelation order and period — a scholarly convention, not a documented record, and early-manuscript evidence complicates any precise sequencing. Name counts are computed from the Leeds corpus's proper-noun tags; romanized labels are editorial working labels. No sirah or asbab al-nuzul source is registered on this site yet (see Sources) — the sirah worksheet is blank scaffolding, and your answers are saved in this browser, never auto-filled, and never carry a verification badge.
